newsitem.title: UK: Musical "Tommy" leads UK theatre award nominations.
newsitem.headline: Musical "Tommy" leads UK theatre award nominations.

text.p: "Tommy", the musical about "the deaf, dumb and blind kid who sure plays a mean pinball," on Tuesday led the field when Britain's theatreland announced nominations for its annual awards.
Pete Townshend's classic, first performed by The Who in 1969, was in line for eight Laurence Olivier awards with Paul Keating nominated as best actor in a musical.

"It's brilliant. It is what it deserves," said Keating, who was stacking shelves in a London supermarket before he auditioned for the hit musical. "I still love it because I have all the good songs to sing."

Roger Daltrey, whose stage presence and voice helped turn The Who into one of the world's great rock acts in the 1970s, played Tommy in the film. The part requires the star to age dramatically and play half the show struck deaf, dumb and blind.

London's West End, currently enjoying an audience boom, attracts eight million visitors a year. Musicals dominate the London stage with Andrew Lloyd Webber hits like "Cats" and "Sunset Boulevard" attracting the biggest crowds.

But heavyweight theatre was recognised in the award choices with Diana Rigg and David Suchet nominated in the best actress and actor categories for a much-acclaimed revival of Edward Albee's "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?"

"I think serious theatre can survive in the West End but it tends to be revivals and the most famous ones at that," said Suchet after accepting his nomination for the awards that will be announced on February 16.

Suchet, who won international acclaim as the detective Hercule Poirot, said: "Theatre is in a very healthy state at the moment. It's the biggest renaissance since the Thirties. It is a wonderful time."
But he conceded that the stage could face tough times: "We have to somehow re-educate young people to come to the theatre in a very television and film-oriented age."
Oscar-winning classical actor Paul Scofield, nominated for Ibsen's "John Gabriel Borkman" at the Royal National Theatre, insisted: "There is an appetite for serious theatre."
"It has never been like a football audience. It has always been smaller, but it is there," he told Reuters. But he complained: "There are too many musicals, all with the same tunes."
